title: Indienne Opens in Hudson Yards: Inside America's Most Ambitious Indian Tasting Menu
excerpt: Michelin-starred chef Sujan Sarkar is opening not one but three Indian dining concepts in Manhattan, signalling a new chapter for Indian fine dining in the United States.
body:
On May 28, a 34-seat restaurant opened on the second floor of a luxury residential tower in Manhattan's Hudson Yards, and it may well be the most significant Indian restaurant opening in America this year. Indienne New York, the expansion of chef Sujan Sarkar's Michelin-starred Chicago flagship, has arrived in the city that never stops eating — with a $195 tasting menu and an audacious plan to prove that Indian cuisine belongs in the highest echelon of American fine dining.

## From Kolkata to a Michelin Star

Sarkar's journey reads like the arc of Indian food itself in the West. Born in Kolkata, he honed his craft in London's European fine-dining kitchens before moving to the United States, where he opened the modern Indian gastrobar Baar Baar in the East Village in 2017.

But it was Chicago that made his name. When Indienne opened in River North in September 2022, amid the uncertain aftershocks of COVID-19, the idea of a full Indian tasting-menu restaurant at scale felt commercially risky. Sarkar began cautiously, offering an 80% tasting menu alongside a small à la carte section.

"We didn't know if people would accept a fully Indian tasting-menu experience at that scale," he recalled.

Within months, diners answered decisively. By February 2023, Indienne had shifted entirely to tasting menus. Later that year, it earned a Michelin star — becoming the first-ever starred Indian restaurant in the Chicago area and one of only four in the entire country.

## The New York Bet

The Hudson Yards outpost is no simple transplant. Sarkar is opening three distinct concepts inside Henry Hall at 515 West 38th Street. Indienne New York anchors the second floor, offering nine-course tasting menus in non-vegetarian ($195), vegetarian ($175), and vegan formats. The experience begins with chaat-inspired courses before progressing into seasonal dishes that highlight layered spices, regional Indian influences, and varied textures.

On the ground floor, Elder — a British-Indian chophouse named after elderflower, an ingredient common to both South Asian and British cuisines — will serve dry-aged meats, seafood, and gin-centric cocktails. Apas, a cocktail bar named after the Sanskrit word for water, rounds out the trio with South Asian-inflected drinks featuring botanicals and florals.

The interiors, designed in collaboration with MAPA Mueller, blend warmth and sophistication: textured finishes, sculptural lighting, and blush-toned seating surround Holi-inspired paintings by Chicago artist Ken Andjulis.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, Indienne represents something that was long overdue: an Indian restaurant playing confidently on the same field as the French and Japanese fine-dining temples of Manhattan.

"I wanted to come back to New York with something new and more progressive," Sarkar said. "Coming back with Indienne feels like both a homecoming and a new beginning."

The timing is not accidental. Indienne's New York launch arrives as Indian cuisine is experiencing an unprecedented moment in America. Cal-India Collective and Chai Pani Restaurant Group are James Beard Award finalists for Outstanding Restaurateur. Tamba in Las Vegas earned a Best New Restaurant nomination. Tapori in Washington, DC, has its chef, Suresh Sundas, competing for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic.

Sarkar himself was a James Beard finalist for Best Chef: Great Lakes in both 2024 and 2025. His expanding empire — which now also includes Nadu, Baar Baar in Los Angeles, and Tiya in San Francisco — is proof that the demand exists at every price point and format.

## What's Next

Elder and Apas are expected to open later this summer. Sarkar has also signalled plans for a second location of Nadu in Phoenix and the new Ayra in Chapel Hill, North Carolina.

For NRIs who have watched Indian food slowly climb the American dining ladder, Indienne's arrival in Hudson Yards — alongside a $175 vegan tasting menu, a British-Indian chophouse, and a Sanskrit-named cocktail bar — feels like a milestone. The butter chicken still tastes like butter chicken. It just looks different now, and the rest of New York is finally paying attention.
